overview: Mamenchisaurus was a massive herbivorous sauropod dinosaur famous for possessing one of the longest necks relative to body size of any known animal, with the neck comprising nearly half the total body length. It lived during the Late Jurassic, approximately 160–145 million years ago, with some species possibly extending into the Early Cretaceous, in the Sichuan Basin and Yunnan Province of China. Various species ranged from roughly 15 to 26 metres in length, with some fragmentary evidence suggesting individuals potentially approaching 35 metres.

Named by Young (C.C. Yang) in 1954 based on material from Mamenchi Ferry on the Jinsha River in Sichuan, Mamenchisaurus belongs to the Mamenchisauridae, a family of Eurasian sauropods characterised by extremely elongated necks with numerous cervical vertebrae. Numerous species have been assigned to the genus over the decades, though the validity of many of these species assignments has been questioned and the taxonomy remains partially unsettled.

articles.title: Discovery and Naming
articles.body: The type species Mamenchisaurus constructus was named by C.C. Young (Yang Zhongjian) in 1954, based on a partial skeleton found at the Mamenchi Ferry construction site on the Jinsha River in Sichuan Province. Young named the genus after the ferry crossing, and constructus refers to the construction works that led to its discovery. Young and Zhao described a second species in 1972, M. hochuanensis, known from four nearly complete skeletons and celebrated for its famously elongated neck.

articles.title: The Extraordinary Neck
articles.body: The neck of Mamenchisaurus is among the longest known of any animal, proportionally or absolutely. M. hochuanensis had a neck estimated at 9 metres in a 15-metre animal, while the fragmentary M. sinocanadorum may have had an even longer neck on a body potentially approaching 26 metres or more. The necks were stiffened by overlapping ribs on the cervical vertebrae, limiting lateral flexibility but potentially allowing extensive vertical reach for high browsing.

articles.title: Species Diversity and Taxonomy
articles.body: More than ten species have been assigned to Mamenchisaurus, but many of these assignments have been questioned due to inadequate material or insufficient diagnostic characters. Species such as M. anyuensis, from the Early Cretaceous, push the temporal range of the genus unusually late if correctly assigned, while the geologic age of several Shaximiao Formation species remains debated. Reassessment and revision of Mamenchisaurus taxonomy is ongoing.

articles.title: Mamenchisauridae and Asian Sauropod Biogeography
articles.body: Mamenchisaurus belongs to Mamenchisauridae, a family of long-necked sauropods largely confined to Asia during the Jurassic. The family's restriction to Asia suggests that mamenchisaurids were part of an endemic Asian sauropod radiation that was partly isolated from the Neosauropoda lineages that dominated elsewhere. Understanding mamenchisaurid relationships helps clarify how Jurassic sauropod diversity was structured across Laurasian and Gondwanan landmasses.

record.description: Mamenchisaurus is a historically broad genus of long-necked Chinese eusauropods. The type species M. constructus is based on a partial skeleton from the Sichuan Basin; other named species differ greatly in completeness and may not form a natural genus.
facts: Several species preserve substantial skeletons, but no single completeness claim applies to the whole genus.
The extraordinary neck length is directly supported in some species; the largest whole-body estimates depend on scaling incomplete individuals.
A 2023 analysis recovered named Mamenchisaurus species in a non-monophyletic series, requiring genus-level revision.

presentation.heroLead: The extraordinarily long-necked sauropods of Jurassic China, a genus of several species whose necks could make up half the length of the animal.

animalParagraphs: Mamenchisaurus was a large four-legged plant-eater with a neck longer, relative to its body, than in almost any other sauropod. In M. hochuanensis, known from a nearly complete skeleton, nineteen neck vertebrae make up a neck about nine metres long on an animal of roughly twenty-two metres; the type species M. constructus was smaller, around thirteen metres, and the fragmentary M. sinocanadorum may have carried a neck of fifteen metres or more.

The neck vertebrae are lightly built, with long overlapping neck ribs that stiffened the neck into a beam rather than a flexible hose. The skull, known well only in M. youngi, is short and deep with spoon-shaped teeth suited to cropping foliage. Some individuals preserve a small tail club of fused vertebrae whose function is not known.

How the neck was held is debated. Biomechanical modelling suggests a gently inclined posture with the head raised well above the shoulders, giving access to a wide feeding envelope, but the animal could not have lifted its neck vertically. The different species come from separate rock units and ages, and it is not certain that they all belong in one genus.
animalHighlights: Up to nineteen cervical vertebrae, more than in almost any other dinosaur, are directly counted in the M. hochuanensis skeleton.
Long, overlapping cervical ribs that braced the neck are preserved in several species.
A short, deep skull with spoon-shaped teeth, known from the M. youngi skeleton, differs from the lighter skulls of diplodocids.

lifeCards.label: Feeding
lifeCards.level: Supported by teeth and skull anatomy
lifeCards.reason: Spoon-shaped teeth and a deep snout indicate browsing on foliage. Which plants it ate and how high it habitually fed are inferred from neck modelling rather than observed.

lifeCards.label: Movement
lifeCards.reason: Columnar fore- and hindlimbs are preserved in M. hochuanensis and M. youngi. Speed and gait beyond a walk are not measurable.

lifeCards.label: Known size
lifeCards.reason: M. hochuanensis and M. youngi are measurable from near-complete skeletons; figures for M. sinocanadorum and the type species involve scaling from partial material.

lifeCards.label: Appearance
lifeCards.level: Skin, colour and neck posture reconstructed
lifeCards.reason: Body proportions come from articulated skeletons. Skin texture, colour and the habitual angle of the neck are inferred.

locality.name: Mamingxi (Mamenchi) construction site
locality.note: Shaximiao Formation. The type species was found during dam construction in 1952; later species come from Hechuan, Zigong and other Sichuan Basin sites and from the Junggar Basin of Xinjiang.

presentation.classificationSummary: Mamenchisaurus is a eusauropod and the name-bearing genus of Mamenchisauridae, a mainly Chinese group of long-necked sauropods outside Neosauropoda. The many species assigned to it were recovered as a non-monophyletic series in 2023, so the genus is probably in need of splitting.

related.reason: A fellow Sichuan mamenchisaurid with a similarly long neck, often confused with Mamenchisaurus in older accounts.
A shorter-necked, tail-clubbed sauropod from the same Shaximiao succession for comparison.
A neosauropod that evolved a long neck independently, with a very different skull and tooth form.

questions.title: Is Mamenchisaurus one genus?
questions.copy: At least seven species have been assigned to it from different rock units and ages. A 2023 analysis found them scattered across the mamenchisaurid tree, so several may need new genus names.

questions.title: How long was the longest neck?
questions.copy: M. sinocanadorum is known chiefly from skull bones and a few neck vertebrae. Its estimated fifteen-metre neck depends on scaling those bones against more complete relatives.

questions.title: How was the neck held?
questions.copy: Biomechanical models suggest a raised but not vertical posture. Direct evidence of habitual posture is unavailable, and different models give different answers.

review.ageReviewNote: The range is restricted to well-supported Middle-Late Jurassic Chinese species; Early Cretaceous and non-Chinese referrals are not used to extend it.

panel.headline: A partial type skeleton and several near-complete referred skeletons, spread across a genus that may not be natural.
panel.standfirst: Mamenchisaurus is well represented as a whole, but unevenly. The type species M. constructus rests on a partial skeleton found during dam construction in 1952, while M. hochuanensis and M. youngi are known from articulated skeletons, and other species from far less.

coverage.label: Good
coverage.basis: Most skeletal regions, including the skull, are known from articulated skeletons, but they come from different species, and the type species itself is only partially known.

metrics.label: Individuals
metrics.value: Several, across at least 7 named species

knownRemains.title: What is actually preserved?
knownRemains.summary: The type species preserves vertebrae, including part of the neck, with ribs, pelvic and limb elements. M. hochuanensis adds a near-complete postcranial skeleton with nineteen cervicals and a tail club; M. youngi adds a near-complete skeleton with skull. M. sinocanadorum is represented by skull bones and a few neck vertebrae.
knownRemains.note: Because the best skull, the best neck and the type material belong to different species, no single individual shows the whole animal, and measurements should not be combined across species.

materialGroups.label: Skull and jaws
materialGroups.value: A nearly complete skull and lower jaws in M. youngi; skull bones and teeth in M. sinocanadorum. No skull is known for the type species.

materialGroups.label: Vertebral column
materialGroups.value: Complete or near-complete cervical, dorsal, sacral and caudal series in M. hochuanensis and M. youngi, with a tail club in some individuals; partial series in the type species.

materialGroups.label: Girdles and limbs
materialGroups.value: Pectoral and pelvic girdles and complete limbs in M. hochuanensis and M. youngi; partial girdle and limb elements in M. constructus.

materialGroups.label: Exceptional preservation
materialGroups.value: Fused tail-club vertebrae are preserved in M. hochuanensis. No skin impressions, colour or gut contents are known.

interpretation.label: Directly observed
interpretation.value: Articulated skeletons with up to nineteen neck vertebrae, long cervical ribs, columnar limbs, a deep skull in one species and a tail club in another.

interpretation.label: Scientific interpretation
interpretation.value: A radiation of very long-necked eusauropods that browsed over a wide feeding envelope, with necks braced by overlapping ribs rather than held flexibly.

interpretation.label: Still unknown
interpretation.value: Whether the named species form one genus, the true size of the most fragmentary species, habitual neck posture, and the function of the tail club.
